awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: The Development of Monumental Architecture
awd_abstract_narration:
Studies of early monumental architecture have traditionally focused on the scale of buildings and their final configuration, often employing a quantitative perspective. This doctoral dissertation project integrates additional analytical frameworks to assess the emergence of monumental works as a process that articulates different levels of analysis over time. The research sheds new light on one of the most critical periods in history when large, monumental constructions flourished before the rise of states, offering a new case study on how societies achieved monumentality as a process unrelated to top-down state-sponsored works. The project provides training for a graduate student in scientific methods of data collection and analysis, and builds capacity for future scientific research. 

This doctoral dissertation project evaluates the emergence of monumental architecture, the associated social practices, and the role that competition and corporate organizations played during the construction of ritual spaces. This period saw the regional rise of massive pyramidal complexes with an enigmatic U-shaped architectural pattern. Using archaeology and geospatial analysis, a monumental U-shaped ritual complex is studied to understand its architectural design, spatial organization, and construction practices over time. Four questions guide this research: (1) What types of activities took place in the different buildings, and how did different social groups participate in them? (2) how did the structures change over time? (3) what role did the structures play in existing interregional interaction and exchange spheres? and (4) on a regional scale, how does the distribution of U-shaped structures reveal patterns of societal organization? To address these questions, the research conducts excavations in different site areas, analyzes the different cultural assemblages, examines the changes in the architecture and constructive techniques, and compiles a geospatial database of other U-shaped structures.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project investigates one of the oldest monumental ceremonial centers on the central coast of Peru: The San Jacinto temple in the Chancay Valley. Occupied between the second and first millennia BCE—centuries before the Inca Empire—the site sheds new light on the early development of monumental architecture in the region. Through archaeological excavations, architectural analysis, mapping, scientific dating, and complementary geospatial technologies, the research demonstrates that the temple was conceived as a monumental structure from the outset. Rather than being built all at once, it developed over multiple stages, with earlier buildings carefully buried to make way for new ones as part of a recurring ritual practice.

Over time, this process generated increasing architectural complexity through a sequence of superimposed constructions that consistently reproduced the same design, pointing to enduring and widely shared principles of organization. The study also documents, for the first time in the Chancay Valley, the temple’s formal façade, offering new insight into the spatial logic of this architectural tradition. Scientific dating further indicates that the site remained active throughout much of this period, underscoring its long-term significance within the regional landscape. A broader geospatial perspective situates San Jacinto as a sacred node within an interconnected network of centers that shared similar architectural and ritual frameworks. Taken together, these findings highlight a sustained and coordinated process of construction in which monumentality emerged through collective practices maintained over generations, pointing to forms of large-scale organization grounded in cooperation and shared ritual commitments.

Beyond its scientific contributions, the project also had a meaningful local impact. Community members participated in fieldwork and site preservation efforts, and students received training in archaeological methods and digital documentation—contributing both to advancing knowledge and to the protection of cultural heritage.
